area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly a stabilized approach to a chosen spot, correct for crosswind, avoid wake turbulence, flare and touch down within ACS tolerances, and go around early when it is not working.
why: The landing phase causes more pilot-caused accidents than any other single phase of flight [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. A planned, stable approach makes good landings routine and makes the go-around decision easy.

prereading.what: Flaps, the five phases, stabilized approach, round out, touchdown, rollout, common errors, go-arounds.

warmup: You are on a 2-mile final, a little fast and a little high, with a gusty crosswind. A regional jet just landed ahead of you. What are the three things you would check, and at what point would you go around?

key_terms.def: Stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, at a constant airspeed and configuration.
The spot you would hit if you never flared. It does not move in the windshield.
The slow, smooth change from approach attitude to landing attitude, a few inches above the runway.
Heading turned into the wind so the ground track stays on centerline; crab removed with rudder just before touchdown.
Rudder keeps the nose on centerline; upwind wing lowered with aileron just enough to stop drift.
The difference between the steady wind and the gusts. Pilots often add half of it to approach speed.
Two counter-rotating vortices that trail from the wingtips of any aircraft making lift.
A normal maneuver to stop an approach or landing: power, attitude, then configuration.
Land and Hold Short Operations: landing and stopping before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or set point.

chunks.title: Five phases and a good base leg

body.p: The AFH splits the end of every landing into five phases: base leg, final approach, round out (flare), touchdown, and after-landing roll [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. A normal approach is for power available, light wind or wind straight down the runway, no obstacles, and a firm, long runway. Pick a landing point past the threshold but within the first 1/3 of the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

bullets: Before-landing checklist (and gear down, if retractable) done before you reach base leg [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Base leg placement sets up the whole approach. Strong headwind on final or steep flap setting? Put base closer to the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
On base: reduced power, target about 1.4 VSO. Example: VSO 60 kt, so 1.4 x 60 = 84 kt [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Crab into the wind on base so your ground track stays square to the extended centerline [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Full flaps are not recommended until final is established [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

body.p: Flaps add lift and drag. They allow a slower, steeper approach, a lower nose for better view, and a shorter roll. Up to about 15 degrees mostly adds lift (the airplane may balloon); beyond 15 degrees adds a lot of drag [[24:172|AFH 9-1]] [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Add flaps in steps on downwind, base, and final, and re-trim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

callout.text: Your POH speeds and flap settings come first. The AFH says the manufacturer's procedures take precedence over its general guidance [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

check.q: Your VSO is 50 kt. What base-leg speed does the AFH suggest as a target?
check.a: About 1.4 VSO = 70 kt, unless your POH says otherwise [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, flown at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Use the POH approach speed, or 1.3 VSO if there is none, and trim off the pressure [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

Energy management = pitch and power together. Too high: reduce power and lower the nose to hold airspeed (or add flaps). Too low: add power and raise the nose [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Raising the nose alone to stretch a glide is almost always a bad idea; it bleeds airspeed and can cause a big sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

Reading the picture: the aiming point does not move in the windshield. If it moves down (away from the horizon) you will land long; if it moves up toward the horizon you will land short [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. On a steady glide path the runway keeps the same shape. Too shallow, it looks shorter and wider; too steep, longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

head: AFH stabilized criteria (typical piston airplane)
Target
rows: About a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone
Tracks centerline; bank normally no more than 15 degrees once on final
+10/-5 KIAS of the AFM speed or 1.3 VSO
Landing flaps as needed, gear down, in trim
Generally 500-1,000 fpm; if over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL
Not below the AFM minimum for approach
Done before the approach (except the landing checklist)

body.p: Source for the table: [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: Go-around gates: not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC (1,000 ft in IMC) means go around. In a typical piston pattern, go around immediately if the approach goes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Pitch for the spot, power for the speed... but always move them together. Never fix a low approach by pulling back alone or by raising flaps [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

check.q: On final, the spot you are aiming at is moving up toward the horizon. What does that mean and what do you do?
check.a: You are going to land short. Add power and raise the nose together to shallow the descent, keeping airspeed [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Where you look matters. Keep your head natural and move your focus from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back. Look too close and you round out high and drop in; look too far and you may fly into the runway nose first [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. As the flare starts, look ahead at a shallow 10 to 15 degree angle to the runway [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].

Start the round out about 10 to 20 feet above the ground. Raise the nose slowly so the airplane keeps settling while it slows [[24:179|AFH 9-8]]. Reach landing attitude and touchdown speed at the same moment the wheels touch. With full flaps the nose has farther to travel, so raise it a bit faster [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].

bullets: Once the flare starts, do not push forward. Too much back pressure? Relax it slightly or hold it, and add a little power if sinking fast [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
Keep one hand on the throttle the whole approach and landing [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
Touch down on the mains at or just above stall speed, nose wheel held off [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
No brake pressure at touchdown. Hold back pressure, then let the nose wheel down gently as you slow [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
Longitudinal axis must be parallel to the direction of travel at touchdown, or you put side loads on the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
The landing is not over until you are at taxi speed or stopped clear of the runway. Use rudder, then nose wheel steering, then brakes as needed [[24:180|AFH 9-9]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

callout.text: Do the after-landing checklist only after you are clear and stopped. Positively identify the flap control before you move it; pilots have raised the gear instead of the flaps on the rollout [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

check.q: Why should brakes not be engaged at touchdown?
check.a: Early braking can drop the nose suddenly and lose aerodynamic braking [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and the ACS tolerances)

body.p: Generic AFH flow. Use your POH numbers for speeds and flaps.

bullets: 1. Downwind: before-landing checklist complete before base; radio call [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
2. Base: reduce power, target about 1.4 VSO, flaps as recommended, crab to hold a square ground track; radio call [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
3. Turn final: coordinated, no more than about 30 degrees of bank near the ground, no skid. Align with the centerline [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].
4. Verify it is the right runway (number, alignment) and scan it for traffic and obstacles [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
5. Final flaps, pitch and power for POH speed (or 1.3 VSO), trim. Pick the aiming point [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].
6. Fly stabilized: scan aiming point, horizon, runway sides, short of the runway, and the airspeed indicator [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
7. Crosswind: wing-low, rudder keeps the nose on centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
8. At 10-20 ft, power to idle and round out smoothly [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].
9. Touch down on the mains, no drift, aligned, in landing attitude [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
10. Rollout: hold back pressure, ailerons into the wind, steer with rudder, brake gently after the nose wheel is down [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
11. Exit at the first available taxiway and cross the hold-short markings; then after-landing checklist [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Any time it is not stable or not safe: go around (power, attitude, configuration) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: What the examiner checks
ACS tolerance
rows: POH approach speed, or if none, not more than 1.3 VSO; +10/-5 knots, with gust factor applied (ACS PA.IV.B.S7)
On, or within 400 feet beyond, the specified point (ACS PA.IV.B.S10)
Proper pitch attitude, no side drift, longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS PA.IV.B.S10)
Timely, if the approach cannot meet these tolerances or anything makes it unsafe (ACS PA.IV.B.S11)

callout.text: No crosswind on checkride day? The examiner must test crosswind knowledge orally (ACS PA.IV.B note).

check.q: The examiner picks the 1,000-foot markers as your point. Where may you touch down?
check.a: On the markers or up to 400 feet beyond them, with no drift and aligned with centerline (ACS PA.IV.B.S10).

body.p: There are two methods: crab and wing-low (sideslip). The wing-low method is recommended in most cases, and you can combine them: crab on a long final, then change to wing-low before the round out. Learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

head: Crab
Wing-low (sideslip)
rows: Turn the heading into the wind so the ground track follows centerline
Rudder holds the nose on centerline; lower the upwind wing just enough to stop drift
Remove the crab with rudder the instant before touchdown; early or late = side load
Hold the correction; land on the upwind main wheel first

bullets: As you slow in the flare, controls get less effective. Add more aileron and rudder to keep the same correction. Keep the upwind wing down [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
With rudder-linked nose wheel steering, relax the rudder as the nose wheel touches so you do not swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On the rollout the airplane wants to weathervane into the wind. Steer with rudder and keep adding aileron into the wind; when stopping, hold it fully into the wind [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

body.p: Limits: airplanes are tested to be controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO. Airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 show this demonstrated crosswind on a placard [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Use a crosswind component chart to find headwind and crosswind components [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

callout.text: If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn while you hold the needed bank, the wind is too strong for that runway. Use a better runway or another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

check.q: Wind is from the right on final using wing-low. Which wing is down, and which rudder are you holding?
check.a: Right wing down, left rudder to keep the nose on centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

chunks.title: Wind, gusts, wind shear, and the runway

body.p: You land at the same indicated airspeed in any wind, so wind changes your groundspeed at touchdown, and that changes runway used [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Headwind shortens the landing; tailwind makes it much longer.

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Tailwind up to 10 kt: add 10% for each 2 kt [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]]
Every 10 ft above 50 ft at the threshold
200 ft longer (100 ft crossing height = +1,000 ft) [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]
Same IAS but higher TAS; 5,000 ft is about 16% longer than sea level [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]

body.p: Surface: water reduces braking, and hydroplaning tires ride on water with almost no braking or steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Minimum hydroplaning speed is about 9 x the square root of tire pressure; 36 psi gives 54 kt [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. On a wet runway, land into the wind, avoid abrupt inputs, and use aerodynamic braking [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Snow, ice, or soft ground has a big effect on landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. A slippery runway plus a tailwind is extra risky [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

Gusts and turbulence: fly a power-on approach slightly faster than normal, often normal speed plus half the gust factor (70 kt with 15 kt gusts = 77 kt), with partial flaps in gusty crosswinds. Close the throttle only after the mains touch [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction. Headwind changing to tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst on approach can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind, and push you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Be ready to go around at the first sign; some microbursts cannot be escaped [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

Don't count on a headwind warning first: microbursts are often lopsided, so the airspeed gain may be small or missing [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. A rapid, large airspeed increase near convective weather may mean a loss is coming and can be a reason to stop the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. If you pull power and lower the nose for that gain, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. A stabilized approach makes bad trends easier to spot [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

callout.text: Virga with an intense rain shaft, or a ring of blowing dust, may be the only visible clue of a microburst [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Near thunderstorms, delay or divert; once on approach, go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

check.q: Your POH says 1,200 ft to land (no wind). You cross the threshold at 100 ft instead of 50 ft. Roughly how much more runway?
check.a: About 1,000 ft more (200 ft per extra 10 ft of height) [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

body.p: Every aircraft making lift leaves two counter-rotating wingtip vortices. They can roll a small airplane faster than its ailerons can fight [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]]. The strongest come from aircraft that are HEAVY, CLEAN, and SLOW [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]].

bullets: Wake starts at rotation and ends at touchdown [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
Vortices sink several hundred feet per minute. Fly at or above the larger aircraft's path [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
Near the ground (within 100 to 200 ft) they spread sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].
A 1 to 5 knot crosswind can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone. A tailwind can push vortices forward into it. The light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

head: Landing behind a larger aircraft...
Do this (AIM 7-4-6)
rows: Stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Landing, parallel runway closer than 2,500 ft
Consider drift to your runway; stay at or above its path; note its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Note its rotation point; land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After its low approach, missed approach, or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before you land or take off [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]

body.p: A tower may say "CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE," but warning or not, you must adjust your flight path to avoid it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Accepting traffic information, an instruction to follow, or a visual approach means you accept wake separation responsibility [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]. Stay out of 3 rotor diameters of a hovering helicopter [[34:153|AIM 7-4-7]].

callout.text: Above and beyond: stay ABOVE its glide path, land BEYOND its touchdown point.

check.q: A large jet just did a touch-and-go on your runway with a light quartering tailwind. What does the AIM say?
check.a: The vortex can stay on the runway and in your path. Wait at least 2 minutes before landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

chunks.title: Picking the runway, go-arounds, and LAHSO

body.p: Choose the runway and touchdown spot for your skill, the airplane, the distance, and the wind. Check the crosswind component against the demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]], compute landing distance from the POH, and add margin for real life; AC 91-79B uses a 15% safety margin [[27:37|AC 91-79B Fig 5-1]]. Slope and surface data are in the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
Plan every approach as a possible go-around. It is a normal maneuver, not a failure [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Two things delay it: landing expectancy ("it'll work out") and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Go-around step
What to do
rows: Full (or max allowable) power, smoothly, right away; carb heat off if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Forward pressure to stop the nose rising, right rudder for torque/P-factor, rough trim; do not climb out of ground effect too soon [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Flaps up in small steps; gear up only after positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

body.p: Go around for: unstable approach, can't land in the first third or drifting [[24:203|AFH 9-32]], big balloon or bad bounce [[24:204|AFH 9-33]] [[24:205|AFH 9-34]], wrong runway doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]], wind shear or wake turbulence [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

LAHSO: tower may clear you to land and hold short of a runway, taxiway, or point. Accept only if you can land and stop in the Available Landing Distance (ALD) [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. The PIC can decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

bullets: Once accepted, you must comply like any clearance; a rejected landing is still allowed [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].
Exit before the hold-short point or stop at it. If you go around, keep clear of other traffic and tell the tower [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].
Read back the clearance with the words "HOLD SHORT OF ..." [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].
LAHSO needs at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: Name the three go-around steps in order.

chunks.title: Traffic, radios, right runway, and low-altitude traps

body.p: Collision hazards: aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way. When two are landing, the lower one has it, but may not cut in front of one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Straight-in traffic has no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]]. High wings block the view above, low wings below; worst case is a low wing above a high wing [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

Radio calls at a non-towered airport: monitor and announce about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], then "left downwind," "left base," and "on final for runway [XX]" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Do not announce your sequence number [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1 Note]], and avoid the words "to" and "for" that can be mistaken for numbers [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.3]].

Right runway: wrong-surface landings come from unfamiliar airports, complacency, or fatigue. Study the airport diagram first; on every final check runway number and alignment. If in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

Runway incursions after landing: exit at the first available taxiway, never onto another runway without ATC approval. You are clear only when all of the airplane is past the hold-short markings [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

Low altitude stall/spin: the classic is an overshoot of the base-to-final turn with a tailwind on base. Pilot adds bank, back pressure, and inside rudder: a skidding, cross-controlled stall that can spin. Do not skid; keep bank at about 30 degrees or less; go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

CFIT is one of the top four causes of GA fatal accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Illusions: a narrow or upsloping runway makes you feel high so you fly too low; a wide or downsloping runway the opposite [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Featureless terrain, rain, and haze also cause low approaches [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Low finals need power and pitch, not flap retraction [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

Distractions: do checklists early so your eyes are outside during the approach [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Many distractions start small (a gauge reading wrong) and lead to accidents when the pilot stops flying the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Task saturated? Stop, think, slow down, and prioritize; or just go around.

callout.text: Aviate, then navigate, then communicate. On short final, flying the airplane is the only job.

check.q: You overshoot the turn to final. What is the safest fix?
check.a: Go around; do not tighten the turn with inside rudder (skid) [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: AFH list of common normal-landing errors [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]: late checklist, poor base drift correction, bad turn to final, skidding turn, unstable approach, not compensating for flaps, poor trim, using elevator alone, focusing too close or too far, touching down before landing attitude, not holding back pressure, excessive braking, loss of control.

head: Problem
Fix
rows: Add power and raise the nose together; never retract flaps. In doubt, go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Flaps, less power, lower the nose; or forward slip. Sink rate over 800-1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power right away; if slow and low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Hold the attitude until it settles; maybe a little power. Big nose-down needed? Go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Ease into landing attitude as it settles; not in the first third or drifting? Go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Some power to cushion; keep crosswind correction. Excessive? Go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]] [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Slight: power to cushion and set landing attitude. Severe: go around now [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Same as bounce; severe or worsening = go around [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Smooth back pressure; go around if able [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]
Touchdown in a drift or crab
Use wing-low; drifting touchdown can damage gear or cause a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]

body.p: Crosswind errors include landing in winds beyond the demonstrated value, releasing the correction, touching down drifting, and too much speed [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

callout.text: A 6-inch drop is roughly a 340 fpm descent onto the gear [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. Hold it off; don't drop it in.

check.q: After a hard bounce the nose is high and airspeed is dropping fast. Land or go around?
check.a: Go around immediately: full power, keep straight, lower the nose to a safe climb attitude [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

scenario.title: Gusty afternoon behind a jet
scenario.setup: You are a student pilot on a solo cross-country into a towered airport. ATIS: wind 230 at 12 gusting 22, runway 27 in use, runway 18 also open, recent rain. Your POH approach speed is 65 kt and the placarded demonstrated crosswind is 15 kt. Tower says: "Number two following a regional jet on 2-mile final, caution wake turbulence. Runway 27, cleared to land, hold short of runway 18." There are thunderstorms 20 miles west.

questions.q: Can you accept the hold-short clearance?
questions.a: No. Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate, and the PIC may decline. Tell tower right away and ask for the full length [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: How do you avoid the jet's wake on the same runway?
questions.a: Stay at or above its final approach path, note where it touches down, and land beyond that point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Watch the wind: a light crosswind (1 to 5 kt) or a tailwind can keep vortices in the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

questions.q: What approach speed do you fly?
questions.a: Normal speed plus half the gust factor: gusts are 10 kt over the steady wind, so about 65 + 5 = 70 kt, with power on and partial flaps if your POH allows [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

questions.q: Wet runway and gusts: what changes in your landing plan?
questions.a: Expect weaker braking and possible hydroplaning; land on speed and on the spot, use aerodynamic braking, avoid abrupt inputs [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Extra speed or height eats runway fast [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2-5.2.3]].

questions.q: On short final your airspeed suddenly drops 15 kt and you start sinking. What now?
questions.a: Possible wind shear from the storms. Go around now: full power, proper attitude, then clean up [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: Workload is high. What helps most?
questions.a: Checklists done early, eyes outside; stop, think, slow down, prioritize. If the approach is not stable by 500 ft, go around [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist before base, and the after-landing checklist once clear and stopped.
skills.practice: Say the checklist out loud by the same point on downwind every time.

skills.do: Make correct pattern calls (CTAF) or tower calls and read back hold-short instructions.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the calls for downwind, base, and final; listen to live ATC/CTAF.

skills.do: Line up with the correct/assigned runway.
skills.practice: On every final, say the runway number you see and compare it with the clearance or plan.

skills.do: Scan the runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Build a habit: look at the runway, both ends, and taxiways before turning final and again on short final.

skills.do: Pick a suitable touchdown point for wind, surface, and obstacles.
skills.practice: Before each landing, name your aiming point and touchdown point out loud.

skills.do: Set landing configuration, airspeed, and trim; use pitch and power together to stay stabilized.
skills.practice: Fly approaches at altitude first, then in the pattern, trimming after every flap change.

skills.do: Hold POH approach speed (or not more than 1.3 VSO) +10/-5 kt, gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Glance at the airspeed indicator in every scan cycle on final; call out deviations.

skills.do: Keep directional control and crosswind correction through approach, touchdown, and rollout.
skills.practice: Practice wing-low drift control by flying low along the runway centerline with an instructor.

skills.do: Make a smooth, timely round out and touchdown.
skills.practice: Practice holding the airplane just off the runway as long as possible; move your eyes ahead at a shallow angle.

skills.do: Touch down in landing attitude, within 400 ft beyond or on the point, no drift, aligned on centerline.
skills.practice: Use a fixed marker (e.g., the aiming point markings) and log where you actually touch down.

skills.do: Go around promptly when the approach is out of tolerance or unsafe.
skills.practice: Have your instructor call surprise go-arounds; also practice from very low heights.

skills.do: Use runway incursion avoidance: exit promptly and stop past the hold-short markings.
skills.practice: Brief the exit taxiway before landing; review the airport diagram.

quiz.q: With no manufacturer's recommendation, what final approach speed does the AFH use?
quiz.why: Use the manufacturer's speed or 1.3 VSO [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]. 1.4 VSO is the base-leg target [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: In VMC, typically by what height must the approach be stabilized or you go around?
quiz.why: 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC; 1,000 ft in IMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: On final the runway looks longer and narrower than usual. You are:
quiz.why: A steepened approach makes the runway appear longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

quiz.q: Using the wing-low method, the first wheel to touch down is:
quiz.why: The correction is held through the round out and the upwind main touches first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

quiz.q: Normal approach speed 70 kt, wind gusting 15 kt above steady. A common approach speed is:
quiz.why: Add half the gust factor: 70 + 7.5 is about 77 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

quiz.q: Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway, you should:
options: Fly below its path and land before its touchdown point
Stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point
quiz.why: Stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

quiz.q: A 10-knot tailwind increases landing distance by about:
quiz.why: About 21 percent for the first 10 kt of tailwind [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]] [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a LAHSO clearance is correct?
options: Student pilots should accept it to help traffic flow
Once accepted, a go-around is not allowed
The PIC may decline it, and student pilots should not participate
It can be issued with a 500 ft ceiling
quiz.why: PIC has final authority to accept or decline; student pilots should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Rejected landing is still allowed [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]; minimum 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

takeaways: Set up early: checklist before base, about 1.4 VSO on base, POH speed or 1.3 VSO on final.
Stabilized by 500 ft (VMC) or go around; pitch and power always move together.
Crosswind: wing-low, more control as you slow, upwind main first, ailerons into the wind on rollout.
Tailwind, extra speed, and extra height eat runway fast (10 kt tailwind is about 21% more).
Wake: stay above the larger aircraft's path and land beyond its touchdown point.
A go-around is a normal maneuver: power, attitude, configuration.
cfi_notes: Common student error: chasing the glide path with elevator alone. Have them say 'pitch and power' on every correction.
Teach both crab and wing-low; the AFH recommends wing-low but says current testing standards allow either [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Examiners often pick a touchdown point and watch for floating; excess speed is the usual cause [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
If there is no crosswind on the checkride, crosswind elements are tested orally (ACS PA.IV.B note). Drill the crosswind component chart and the 0.2 VSO idea [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].
Practice go-arounds from low heights and from bounces so the student is not afraid of them; tie it to landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Point out the base-to-final skid trap with a tailwind on base [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Ask: 'What is your go-around trigger today?' before every pattern session.
gaps: Airplane-specific approach speeds, flap settings, demonstrated crosswind, checklists, and landing distance charts are in the POH/AFM, not these resources.
Towered-airport landing phraseology beyond the LAHSO readback example (AIM 4-3-11) is not covered in the pages used.

AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide), cited by the PHAK, was cancelled by the FAA in 2022; this lesson uses the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) instead. AWH 22-10 to 22-18 covers microburst effects, warning signs and the general principle of holding pitch attitude and accepting lower airspeed, but its encounter studies appear to involve large, crew-flown airplanes (crew coordination, stick shakers, aft body contact) and it gives no step-by-step windshear escape procedure for small airplanes. Get the airplane-specific technique from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
The ACS does not define 'gust factor'; the lesson uses the AFH 'half the gust factor' practice (AFH 9-20).
CFIT on approach is covered only indirectly (low-final corrections, landing illusions, RMH accident causes); no dedicated CFIT-on-approach section was found.

activities.title: Too high or too low?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: The runway looks longer and narrower than usual
The aiming point moves down, away from the horizon
Fix: reduce power and lower the nose to hold airspeed
Fix: add more flaps, if you have some left
The runway looks shorter and wider than usual
The aiming point moves up toward the horizon
Fix: add power and raise the nose together
Never fix it by raising the flaps

activities.title: Fly the landing in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Finish the before-landing checklist before you reach base leg
On base, reduce power and slow to about 1.4 VSO
Turn final and line up with the centerline
Set final flaps, fly POH speed (or 1.3 VSO), and trim
At 10 to 20 feet, start a smooth round out
Touch down on the main wheels, nose wheel held off
Let the nose wheel down gently, then brake as needed
Clear the runway past the hold-short markings, then do the after-landing checklist

cards.s: The AFH recommends the crab method for most crosswind landings.
cards.why: No. The wing-low (sideslip) method is recommended in most cases, but you should learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

cards.s: In a crab, you use rudder to line the nose up with the runway the instant before touchdown.
cards.why: Yes. Doing it too early or too late puts a side load on the gear [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

cards.s: As you slow down in the flare, you need less aileron and rudder to hold the same correction.
cards.why: No. The controls get less effective as you slow, so you need more aileron and rudder [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

cards.s: If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn while you hold the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway.
cards.why: Yes. Land on a better runway or at another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

cards.s: As you come to a stop on the rollout, hold the ailerons fully toward the wind.
cards.why: Yes. As you slow, the ailerons work less and the wind lifts the upwind wing more, so you keep adding aileron into the wind [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

cards.s: Before type certification, airplanes are tested to be controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to half of VSO.
cards.why: No. The test goes up to 0.2 VSO, two-tenths of the stall speed in landing configuration [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

activities.title: Dodge the wake
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then what the AIM says to do.

pairs.r: Stay at or above its path, land beyond its touchdown point
Note its rotation point and land well before it

pairs.l: Larger plane just did a touch-and-go
pairs.r: Wait at least 2 minutes before you land
Stay more than 3 rotor diameters away

final_quiz.q: Your POH approach speed is 65 kt and the air is smooth. On the checkride, which airspeed range on final meets the standard?
final_quiz.why: The ACS allows the POH approach speed +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.B.S7): 65 - 5 = 60 kt and 65 + 10 = 75 kt. The AFH uses the same +10/-5 window for a stabilized approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your normal approach speed is 75 kt. The wind is 260 at 8 knots, gusting 20. Using the common AFH rule of thumb, what speed do you fly on final?
final_quiz.why: The gust factor is 20 - 8 = 12 kt. Add half of it: 75 + 6 = 81 kt [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Your POH speeds come first if they say something different.

final_quiz.q: You are flying a piston trainer in the traffic pattern. At 250 ft AGL the approach becomes unstable. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Fix it with elevator alone and land
Keep going if you can still land in the first half of the runway
Raise the flaps to stop the sink
final_quiz.why: For a typical piston airplane in the pattern, go around immediately if the approach becomes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: On final, the spot you are aiming at slowly moves down in the windshield, away from the horizon. If you change nothing, you will:
final_quiz.why: When the aiming point moves down away from the horizon, the real aiming point is farther down the runway, so you will overshoot [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Fix it by reducing power and lowering the nose [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You land with the wind from the left. As you slow down on the rollout, what should you do with the ailerons?
options: Turn them more and more to the left, fully left as you stop
Put them neutral, since you are on the ground
Turn them to the right, away from the wind
Hold left at first, then neutral as you slow
final_quiz.why: Keep the upwind (left) wing from rising. The ailerons get weaker as you slow, so keep adding aileron into the wind, and hold it fully toward the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

final_quiz.q: Before type certification, an airplane must be shown to be controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO. If VSO is 45 kt, that test wind is:
final_quiz.why: 0.2 x 45 = 9 kt [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Look up the demonstrated crosswind for your own airplane and stay within it.

final_quiz.q: Tower clears you to land on runway 9. A business jet is starting its takeoff roll on runway 9 ahead of you. How do you avoid its wake?
options: Land past the point where it lifts off
Note where it rotates and land well before that point
Land anywhere; wake only forms when a plane is landing
final_quiz.why: Wake begins at rotation [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. Behind a larger plane departing the same runway, note its rotation point and land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH landing distance is 1,500 ft. You fly final 10% faster than the POH speed. Using the AC 91-79B rule of thumb, about how much runway will you need?
final_quiz.why: A 10% faster approach means about 20% more landing distance: 1,500 x 1.2 = 1,800 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: Your main tires are inflated to 49 psi. On a wet runway, at about what speed could dynamic hydroplaning start?
final_quiz.why: Minimum hydroplaning speed is about 9 x the square root of tire pressure: the square root of 49 is 7, and 9 x 7 = 63 kt [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

final_quiz.q: You decide to go around at 100 ft AGL and smoothly add full power. What comes next?
options: Raise all the flaps at once
Hold the nose with forward pressure, add right rudder, and rough trim
Pull up hard to climb out of ground effect quickly
Raise the gear, then the flaps
final_quiz.why: After power comes attitude: forward pressure to stop the nose from rising, right rudder for torque and P-factor, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Flaps come up in small steps, and the gear only after a positive rate of climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Why is a skidding turn from base to final so dangerous?
options: It makes the airplane climb above pattern altitude
It always makes the airplane land long
It only matters in tailwheel airplanes
It can cause a cross-control stall and spin close to the ground
final_quiz.why: Bank, back pressure, and inside rudder can cause a cross-control stall that quickly becomes a spin. If you overshoot the turn, go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: You are landing at an unfamiliar airport whose runway slopes uphill. If you do not recognize the illusion, you will tend to:
options: Fly a higher approach than normal
Fly a lower approach than normal
Touch down too fast but on the right path
final_quiz.why: An upsloping runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach and risk landing short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

final_quiz.q: Near a thunderstorm on 1-mile final, your airspeed suddenly jumps 15 kt above normal. What is the best way to treat it?
options: Free energy: pull power and lower the nose to get back on speed
Nothing to worry about, since it is just a gust
It may mean an airspeed loss is coming, so be ready to go around
Good news: a headwind gain always warns you before a microburst
final_quiz.why: A rapid, large airspeed gain near storms may mean a loss is coming and can be a reason to stop the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Be ready to go around at the first sign [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Pulling power and lowering the nose leaves you nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].
